strengths: The paper addresses the useful and challenging problem of referring-expression counting, where models must distinguish visually similar instances using fine-grained attributes and context.

C-REX yields substantial REC-8K improvements: 5.06 MAE and 17.53 RMSE versus GroundingREC's 6.50 and 19.79, while also improving its strong centroid-based baseline from 5.90 to 5.06 MAE. Results broken down by count range and referring-expression category support the aggregate result.

The detection-based formulation provides interpretable point localizations. Qualitative examples show successful discrimination of orientation, location, color, and action, and the supplementary material also presents failure cases.

The ablations compare the proposed loss with the baseline and conventional supervised contrastive loss, and examine several choices for the number of positive tokens. The method also receives limited cross-task evaluation on FSC-147 and CARPK.
weaknesses: The paper's central claim that centroid prediction is the key cause of recent detection-based counting success is not established by a controlled box-versus-centroid experiment. Table 6 simultaneously changes architectural modules, losses, and training, so it cannot isolate centroid prediction.

The mathematical specification appears inconsistent with standard supervised contrastive learning: Equations 1 and 4 place the average over positive probabilities inside a logarithm, whereas the cited supervised contrastive objective averages per-positive log probabilities. This materially changes the optimization behavior, and the paper does not clarify which version was implemented.

Positive labels are assigned to the top-N queries by text-conditioned similarity. This does not ensure distinct queries correspond to distinct ground-truth objects and may select duplicate detections or background. The reported approximately 80% correctness lacks a matching definition, detailed statistics, or comparison with labels derived from the available point annotations.

The characterization of C-REX as operating entirely in image space is overstated: positive selection explicitly uses similarity to masked referring-expression embeddings inside a cross-modal Grounding DINO model. Consequently, the asserted stability advantage over image-text contrastive learning is not directly measured.

Evidence for generality is weak. On FSC-147, gains over GroundingREC are small and C-REX is worse than its own baseline on validation MAE/RMSE; on CARPK, it is worse than the improved baseline and several prior methods. The main REC evidence is confined to one dataset.

Important experimental details needed for reproducibility are missing, including temperature, batch size, training schedule/epochs, augmentation, and seed variance. There are no confidence intervals or repeated-run results, no sensitivity study for the contrastive weight or inference thresholds, and the supplementary discussion contains unresolved citation placeholders.

Overall, this is a promising incremental Algorithms/General contribution with a meaningful empirical result, but ambiguities in the loss definition and insufficient causal validation of the main methodological claims make the current scientific case slightly short of acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful computer-vision problem: distinguishing fine-grained subsets of visually similar objects for referring-expression counting. The manuscript was reviewed in full, including its supplementary material and visual evidence. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/9def21266737430b82ef8b45009208ee/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

On REC-8K, C-REX reports a substantial improvement over GroundingREC: test MAE decreases from 6.50 to 5.06 and RMSE from 19.79 to 17.53. It also improves over the authors' stronger centroid-based baseline, whose test MAE is 5.90.

The ablations examine the modified contrastive objective, the number of selected positive tokens, and components inherited from GroundingREC. The count-range and referring-expression-category breakdowns are useful additions beyond aggregate metrics.

The detection-based formulation produces localized predictions, and the qualitative examples include both successes and failures. This makes the model's behavior more interpretable than count-only regression.
The comparison to the same-backbone GroundingREC method is relevant, while evaluation on FSC-147 and CARPK at least probes whether the training idea transfers beyond REC-8K.
weaknesses: No contribution type is declared, so I assess the submission as Algorithms/General. Under that standard, the algorithmic novelty is limited: the central method applies a supervised-contrastive-style loss to top-N detector tokens, with N supplied by the ground-truth count. The extensions to class-agnostic counting and other tasks are asserted more broadly than demonstrated.

The core claim that C-REX operates 'entirely within the image space' and eliminates image-text misalignment is misleading. Equation 2 selects positives using similarity between image tokens and a masked referring-expression embedding, and the underlying Grounding DINO decoder is cross-modal. Thus, text-image alignment remains essential to the pseudo-label construction even if the final contrastive pairs are image-image.

The loss is insufficiently specified and may be ill-defined for common cases. Equation 1 is not the standard supervised contrastive objective it is presented as: it takes the logarithm after averaging positive exponentials rather than averaging per-positive log probabilities. Equation 4 divides by |I+|-1, but the paper does not explain what happens when the ground-truth count N is zero or one. It also omits the temperature, the precise decoder features being contrasted, masked-text pooling, and handling of duplicate queries assigned to the same object.

The pseudo-label justification is weak. The supplement merely states that about 80% of selected tokens correspond to correct instances, without defining the matching procedure, reporting variation by count or category, or establishing that selected queries represent distinct objects. Treating hundreds of unselected DETR queries—many likely background or redundant—as informative negatives does not by itself establish the claimed advantage over a smaller set of semantically meaningful negatives.

The claim that centroid prediction is the key reason for recent detection-based counting success is not isolated experimentally. Table 6 removes GroundingREC modules sequentially, but it does not present a controlled bounding-box-versus-centroid comparison using otherwise identical initialization, optimization, losses, and thresholds. Evidence from one architecture and dataset also cannot establish the broader causal claim involving CountGD and other methods.

The main evidence is concentrated on REC-8K, the same relatively small benchmark used for training and evaluation. Results lack multiple seeds, uncertainty estimates, significance testing, robustness to thresholds, cross-dataset REC evaluation, and comparisons against simple alternatives such as confidence-weighted positives, Hungarian-matched positives, or a non-contrastive feature regularizer. Consequently, it is unclear how much of the gain is robust or specifically attributable to the proposed contrastive mechanism.

The claimed generality is not convincing. On FSC-147, improvements over prior text-guided models are marginal, C-REX is worse than its own baseline on validation, and visual-exemplar approaches remain substantially better. On CARPK, C-REX is also worse than the authors' baseline and CountGD. These results support limited transfer, not a broadly versatile framework.

The F1 gain over GroundingREC on REC-8K is only 0.01 despite much larger MAE/RMSE improvements, weakening the claim that C-REX markedly improves identification of the correct referred instances rather than primarily count calibration. The exact localization matching protocol for F1 is not documented sufficiently to investigate this discrepancy.

Reproducibility and presentation are below publication standard. The manuscript provides no epochs, batch size, learning-rate schedule, augmentation details, random seeds, temperature, or complete inference/matching specification; its code link is the unresolved phrase 'this url.' The supplement contains unresolved citations '[? ? ?]' and calls an informal argument 'theoretically justified' without supplying a theorem or proof. These are not merely cosmetic because they concern the central training objective and supporting evidence.

Overall, the strong REC-8K numbers are promising, but unresolved objective-definition issues, incomplete reproducibility, insufficient causal ablations, and overstated conceptual and generality claims leave the scientific case short of acceptance. A substantially clarified and more rigorously controlled evaluation could change the assessment.

strengths: Evaluated as an Algorithms/General contribution. The paper addresses the important and relatively new problem of referring-expression counting, where models must distinguish contextually different instances of the same object category.

C-REX is simple and technically intuitive: top-N pseudo-labels derived from the training count are used with a modified supervised contrastive objective that avoids forcing heterogeneous negative tokens together.

The REC-8K results are strong. Relative to GroundingREC, C-REX reduces test MAE from 6.50 to 5.06 (about 22%) and RMSE from 19.79 to 17.53 (about 11%), while improving F1 from 0.69 to 0.70. It also consistently improves over the authors' already-competitive baseline.

The ablations provide useful evidence: the modified loss clearly outperforms both the baseline and conventional supervised contrastive loss, while alternative choices for the number of selected tokens are substantially worse than top-N selection.
Results broken down by count range and referring-expression category, together with localized qualitative predictions and explicit failure cases, make the empirical behavior reasonably transparent.
The extension to class-agnostic counting provides some evidence that the approach is not entirely task-specific, including the best reported test results among text-guided methods on FSC-147.
weaknesses: The claim that centroid prediction is the key reason for the success of recent detection-based counting models is not directly established. Table 6 removes feature-fusion and contrastive modules, but never presents a controlled bounding-box-versus-centroid comparison with the remaining architecture and training protocol fixed.

The explanation that C-REX avoids image-text misalignment is overstated: text-image similarity is still used to select the top-N positive image tokens. Moreover, the paper does not compare its loss against GroundingREC's image-text contrastive loss when both are attached to the same improved baseline, nor ablate the asserted benefit of having more negatives.

Equation 4 is undefined when N=1 because the positive set for an anchor has size |I+|-1=0; N=0 would also be problematic. The manuscript does not explain whether these cases are absent, skipped, or handled through another mechanism. This is an important implementation and reproducibility omission.

The evidence is limited to a single REC dataset, with no repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or statistical testing. The F1 improvement over GroundingREC is only 0.01, so the large count-error reductions do not translate into equally strong evidence of better instance selection.

The broader generality claim is only partially supported. On FSC-147 validation, C-REX is worse than the improved baseline, and on CARPK it is also worse than that baseline (MAE 4.21 versus 3.80). No experiments are provided for the referring segmentation or detection applications suggested in the conclusion.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: training duration, batch size, temperature, scheduling, handling of singleton counts, matching procedure behind the reported 80% top-N correctness, and checkpoint selection are unspecified. The promised code link is not actually embedded in the submitted PDF, and the supplement contains unresolved citation placeholders.

strengths: Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, C-REX is a simple, plausible, and practically useful modification: it replaces image-text contrastive supervision with an intra-image supervised contrastive loss over RE-conditioned visual tokens, requiring no architectural changes.

The main REC evidence is broad and generally convincing. The method is evaluated with GroundingREC, CAD-GD, and GroundingDINO, using both Swin-T and Swin-B backbones. It substantially improves the strongest GroundingDINO configuration on REC-8K, reaching 4.20 MAE and 0.78 F1 on the test set.

The paper includes relevant ablations comparing image-text, image-space, and combined contrastive objectives; alternative positive-token selection strategies; and the proposed positive-anchor-only modification. These experiments support several important design choices.

Evaluation includes localization-aware precision, recall, and F1 in addition to count errors, density-stratified results, paraphrased expressions, qualitative examples, explicit failure cases, and an exploratory extension to FSC-147.
The manuscript is clearly motivated and mostly easy to follow, and it appropriately acknowledges that accurate counts can still arise from localization of the wrong instances.
weaknesses: Equation (2) is undefined when an expression has only one target because |I+|-1 equals zero and there is no positive partner. The manuscript does not state how singleton or empty-target samples are handled, despite such cases being important in counting data. This is a technical and reproducibility gap in the central objective.

The comparison does not cleanly isolate the claimed benefit of the embedding space. C-REX uses ground-truth-conditioned bipartite matching to select positive visual tokens, whereas the image-text objective supplies a structurally different signal. Improvements could therefore arise from token selection or direct point supervision rather than specifically from avoiding image-text alignment. A controlled image-text loss using matched tokens, or image-space losses with alternative supervision held fixed, would strengthen the central conclusion.

Treating every unmatched one of the 900 query tokens as a negative is questionable: unmatched DETR-style queries can include duplicate hypotheses for true objects, background tokens, or poorly localized predictions rather than meaningful objects with different expressions. This creates false negatives, and the paper neither measures their prevalence nor ablates background, duplicate, or hard-negative selection.

The claims of consistent improvement and broad generality are overstated. C-REX worsens some REC validation entries for CAD-GD† and slightly worsens some other metrics. On FSC-147, CAD-GD validation MAE degrades and GroundingREC test MAE increases substantially from 10.12 to 12.46; thus the class-agnostic extension is mixed rather than consistently beneficial.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the proposed loss: the temperature, loss coefficient, optimizer, batch size, normalization/projection details, singleton handling, and random seeds are not reported. Results also lack multiple-run variance or significance estimates, which is especially important for the small gains on several CAD-GD configurations.

Originality is moderate: positive-only supervised contrastive learning over matched object queries is a sensible adaptation of established supervised contrastive and DETR matching ideas, but the paper provides limited representation-level evidence for its explanatory claims. Cluster/separability analyses, alignment measurements, or controlled negative-count experiments would better substantiate the asserted mechanism.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: referring-expression counting requires distinguishing objects with subtle attribute, action, and spatial differences, and the motivation for improving visual-token discrimination is intuitive.
C-REX is simple and potentially useful in practice. It can be inserted into three substantially different counting architectures without changing their inference-time structure.

On REC-8K, the reported improvements are often sizable and occur across Swin-T/Swin-B backbones, multiple architectures, and localization-aware metrics. The strongest GroundingDINO configuration improves test MAE from 5.90 to 4.38 and F1 from 0.68 to 0.75.

The paper includes relevant ablations on image-text versus image-space objectives, positive-token selection, and the modified supervised contrastive loss. Reporting precision, recall, F1, density-stratified results, qualitative examples, and explicit failure cases is also valuable.
The presentation is generally clear, and the relationship to prior REC, counting, and contrastive-learning work is adequately contextualized.
weaknesses: No contribution type is declared, so I assess this as Algorithms/General. The algorithmic novelty is limited: C-REX is essentially a known supervised contrastive objective applied to matched decoder tokens, with negative tokens excluded as anchors. The work does not establish a sufficiently new general contrastive-learning principle beyond this task-specific adaptation.

The main causal claim is not demonstrated. C-REX simultaneously changes the embedding domain, increases the number of negatives, replaces text-derived labels with ground-truth matching, and changes the objective. Consequently, Table 3 cannot establish that the visual embedding space itself is responsible for the gains. Controls with matched negative-set size, hard-negative quality, supervision, and loss form are needed.

The stated interpretation of the loss is questionable. For each language-conditioned image–RE pair, all unmatched tokens are called negatives, but these are not verified to represent different expressions or classes; they can be background, duplicate predictions of a target, or poorly localized tokens. Thus, the objective may primarily improve foreground/background separation or suppress duplicate detections rather than learn the claimed fine-grained inter-expression geometry. No embedding analysis or retrieval/cluster evidence tests the proposed mechanism.

Equation (2) is undefined when an image–expression pair contains only one positive instance because its positive set has size |I+|-1=0. REC examples in the paper include ground-truth counts of one, yet the manuscript never explains how singleton—and potentially zero-count—queries are handled. Other essential details are also missing, including the temperature, loss coefficient, feature normalization, exact matching cost, and handling of unmatched or duplicate tokens. This is a serious soundness and reproducibility omission.

The evidence for generality beyond REC is weak and mixed. On FSC-147, improvements are mostly marginal; CAD-GD validation MAE slightly worsens, and GroundingREC test MAE substantially worsens from 10.12 to 12.46. These results do not support the broad claim that the method consistently benefits class-agnostic counting.

Only one REC dataset is evaluated, and results are reported from apparently single runs without variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Several differences are very small, while comparisons also mix released baseline checkpoints with newly retrained models. This makes consistency and robustness difficult to assess.

The paraphrase experiment is also mixed: CAD-GD degrades substantially with C-REX. The paraphrases are generated by a proprietary model without reporting prompts, quality checks, or semantic-preservation validation, limiting reproducibility and interpretability.

The paper overstates that C-REX eliminates image–text misalignment. The visual tokens are still conditioned on the referring expression through cross-attention, so failures in language representation and cross-modal alignment remain. The provided failure cases indeed show models producing plausible counts for the wrong instances.

Given the narrow novelty, unresolved edge cases in the mathematical definition, missing implementation details, and experiments that do not isolate the claimed mechanism, the empirical gains are insufficient to make a convincing Algorithms/General contribution in the current form.

strengths: The paper presents a simple, well-motivated Algorithms/General contribution: replacing cross-modal contrastive supervision with an intra-image supervised contrastive objective for referring-expression counting. The method is lightweight and can be integrated without architectural changes.

The empirical case on REC-8K is strong. C-REX improves three different architectures across Swin-T and Swin-B backbones, with particularly substantial gains for GroundingREC and GroundingDINO, and achieves state-of-the-art MAE, RMSE, and F1 results.

Evaluation goes beyond count error: precision, recall, F1, count-range breakdowns, localization visualizations, paraphrase testing, and disclosed failure cases provide a reasonably broad picture of behavior.

The ablations support several design decisions, including bipartite-matching-based positive selection, excluding negative samples as anchors, and using image-space supervision instead of combining it with the prior image-text loss.
The paper is clearly organized, appropriately situated relative to REC and class-agnostic counting literature, and candidly shows cases where C-REX fails or does not improve a baseline.
weaknesses: Important implementation details are missing, including the contrastive temperature, loss weight, matching cost, and exact treatment of examples with fewer than two positives. Equation 2 is undefined when the ground-truth count is one, a likely common case, and neither the main paper nor supplement explains how this is handled.

The displayed objective is not the conventional supervised contrastive loss it is described as: it places the positive average inside the logarithm, whereas standard SupCon averages per-positive log probabilities. It is unclear whether this is an intentional variant, a notation error, or the implemented loss, weakening reproducibility.

The experiments do not isolate the paper's central explanation. Moving from image-text to image-only contrast simultaneously changes the embedding space, the construction of positives, and the number and nature of negatives. Controlled negative-count experiments, cross-modal baselines with enlarged negative pools, training-stability measurements, or direct embedding analyses would better establish why the method works.

Some generality and consistency claims are overstated. On FSC-147, GroundingREC+C-REX worsens test MAE from 10.12 to 12.46 and CAD-GD slightly worsens validation MAE; under paraphrasing, CAD-GD+C-REX degrades substantially. Thus transfer and language robustness are architecture-dependent.

All principal REC results come from a single relatively small benchmark, and no multi-seed results, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. This is especially relevant for the smaller CAD-GD gains and the mixed auxiliary-task results.

The method removes text embeddings from the contrastive loss, but its visual tokens remain conditioned on the referring expression through cross-attention. Consequently, the claim that it eliminates image-text misalignment is stronger than the evidence supports; it more precisely avoids using cross-modal pairs as contrastive anchors.

Novelty is moderate—the core technique is a task-specific adaptation of supervised contrastive learning—and computational overhead is not reported. Nevertheless, the breadth and magnitude of the main REC improvements make the contribution useful enough to support acceptance.
